The Satinfin shiner (Cyprinella analostana) is a small-bodied cyprinid native to Atlantic slope drainages of the eastern United States, where it occupies clear, moderate-gradient streams with gravel and cobble substrates. Field surveys indicate that this species reaches a maximum body length of approximately 11 centimeters [Li = approximately 11 centimeters], a size that is typical for members of the genus Cyprinella and reflects the moderate growth potential of these minnows within their preferred lotic habitats. Newly hatched individuals emerge from fertilised eggs at an extraordinarily small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams]. This minute initial mass corresponds to a yolk-dependent larva that relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-eclosion, a critical period during which the chorionate embryo progresses through cleavage and blastula stages before the hatching event. The incubation period is brief, and upon chorion rupture the prolarva emerges as a translucent, non-feeding larva that begins absorbing yolk nutrients and initiating the transition toward first exogenous feeding within a matter of days.

As the prolarvae exhaust their yolk supplies, they undergo the trophic switch to active feeding, marking the onset of the exotrophic larval phase. Growth during the early juvenile period is rapid, but individuals do not reach the pubertal milestone until they have attained a fork length of approximately 4.1 centimeters, which corresponds to a total length at puberty of approximately 4.4 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.4 centimeters]. At this stage of sexual maturation, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 0.68 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.68 grams], a mass that reflects the accumulation of sufficient somatic tissue to support the energetic demands of gonad maturation and the onset of gametogenesis. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a typical power-law allometry, with the body mass at puberty falling well below the asymptotic mass that characterizes fully grown adults. Puberty is thus achieved at a size that represents only a fraction of the ultimate body length, a pattern common among cyprinids that spread reproductive effort across multiple seasons.

Adults of the Satinfin shiner achieve a maximum recorded wet weight of 11.4 grams [Wwi = 11.4 grams], a value derived from the length-weight regression that describes the asymptotic mass plateau for this species. This ultimate wet weight is attained by individuals that have completed their somatic growth trajectory and are reproductively active, typically spawning multiple times during the warmer months. The transition from the juvenile stage to the reproductively viable adult involves not only an increase in body mass by more than an order of magnitude but also the full development of the fin rays, scales, and body plan reorganisation that characterises the post-metamorphic juvenile. Gravid fish are often observed defending nesting territories in shallow riffles, where they broadcast spawn over clean gravel substrates. The species is iteroparous, with adults capable of producing multiple clutches across a single breeding season under favorable thermal conditions.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial when water temperatures are maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a thermal regime that approximates optimal conditions for gonadal recrudescence and spawning activity. Under these laboratory-controlled temperatures, females produce an average of 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch], and they typically complete approximately 1.5 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches annually]. This reproductive schedule yields a total annual fecundity that, when combined with the extended breeding season, allows for considerable population recruitment. Senescence likely sets in after the second or third spawning season, with post-reproductive mortality increasing as individuals exhaust their lipid stores and experience progressive physiological deterioration.
